articleSummary: Schistosomiasis is caused by Schistosoma japonicum, with Oncomelania snails as the sole intermediate host. Humans can become infected by contact with water containing cercariae; even 10 seconds of exposure is enough. Transmission peaks from April to October. Clinical signs include fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fatigue, and hepatosplenomegaly; without timely treatment, progression can lead to liver cirrhosis and ascites. Oncomelania snails are typically under 1 cm and prefer vegetated, clear, slow-moving, moist, organic-rich habitats such as river beaches, dikes, and reed marshes. In China, snails are distributed mainly in the Yangtze River basin and southern river/lake networks near the waterline. Eliminating snails is key to interrupting transmission. This week marks National Schistosomiasis Prevention and Control Week to raise awareness and promote prevention.

articleSummary: On 7 April 2026, CCTV reports that the golden apple snail (Pomacea canaliculata), native to South America, is entering a hatching peak in China. It is one of China’s first 16 harmful invasive species, with annual egg production of 30,000–50,000 per snail and rapid spread that damages rice crops and aquatic plants, threatening farmland and wetlands. Each snail harbors 3,000–6,000 parasites, chiefly Angiostrongylus cantonensis (广州管圆线虫), a neurotropic nematode. In humans, infection can occur by eating contaminated snails, contact with eggs or polluted water, or through skin wounds, causing severe headache, neck stiffness, fever, and vomiting; severe cases may lead to dementia, paralysis, death, or lasting deficits. Between Nov 2025 and Jan 2026, BA.3.2 comprised up to ~30% of sequences in Denmark, Germany, and the Netherlands, and has been identified in at least 23 countries including the United States, United Kingdom, China, and Australia; Brazil has not yet reported this lineage. BA.3.2 carries 70–75 Spike mutations relative to JN.1 and LP.8.1; JN.1 vaccines target JN.1, while WHO recommends adapting vaccines for LP.8.1. No link to higher hospitalizations or deaths; vaccination remains the main protection. Brazil’s vaccination schedule includes pregnant, elderly, and children with boosters for priority groups; general population currently no new doses. Continuous surveillance and maintained vaccination are advised.

articleSummary: Contagiousness of fever with rash infections peaks around rash onset rather than during peak fever. Rash reflects high pathogen levels as the immune system fights the infection. Four common rash illnesses and their transmission: Measles spreads via respiratory droplets or airborne, with the main contagious period around rash onset (about five days before and after). Chickenpox (varicella) spreads by droplets and direct contact and remains contagious from 1–2 days before rash until all lesions crust. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD) transmits through droplets, contaminated objects, or fecal-oral routes; risk is higher about one week after rash onset. Scarlet fever (group A Streptococcus) spreads mainly by droplets, with a potentially prolonged contagious period if untreated. Prevention includes timely isolation, rigorous hand hygiene and environmental cleaning, avoiding school/work during illness, and vaccination (MMR for measles, varicella vaccine, and EV-A71 vaccine for HFMD). Beijing, China.

articleSummary: 61-year-old woman from Lang Son, Vietnam, developed Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis, a serious CNS infection that can affect healthy adults. Working near eucalyptus trees, she likely had environmental exposure to fungal spores and bird droppings. Symptoms—severe headache, dizziness, nausea, high fever—were mistaken for a vestibular disorder. On day six, lumbar puncture confirmed Cryptococcus in the cerebrospinal fluid, and she was transferred in critical condition to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases in Hanoi. After one week, symptoms and CSF inflammation improved, but prolonged treatment and close follow-up are required to prevent relapse. Cryptococcus is common in the environment (bird droppings, decaying trees); infection occurs by inhalation, with CNS involvement in about 85% of cases. Early diagnosis and adherence to therapy are essential.

articleSummary: Measles, caused by Morbillivirus, is a highly contagious respiratory infection. articleSummary: AMR surveillance of typhoidal Salmonella in the Delhi NCR region, India, analyzed more than 10,000 S. enterica isolates from 2020–2024. articleSummary: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) remains a major respiratory pathogen in Brazil, affecting infants and the elderly. As of October 2025, RSV accounted for 40.6% of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SRAG) cases per Fiocruz InfoGripe. RSV spreads via droplets and contaminated surfaces. In healthy adults it resembles a cold; in infants under 2 years it can cause tachypnea, wheeze, respiratory distress, poor feeding, and irritability, potentially bronchiolitis or pneumonia. In older adults and those with chronic diseases it can trigger dyspnea and pneumonia. Diagnosis is clinical; nasal swab testing and imaging may be used for confirmation or complication assessment, with oxygenation checks. Treatment is supportive with hydration, rest, nasal saline, ibuprofen for fever/pain, and nasal decongestants; avoid self-medication in babies. articleHeadline: Why vaccines may not be enough to fight spread of dengue fever
articleSummary: As of 2026-04-07, dengue remains a leading mosquito-borne illness, with outbreaks expanding across Asia, Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Sudan, Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire) and Latin America. Dengue is caused by four serotypes; infection with one usually protects against that type but not others, and antibodies can enhance subsequent infections. Vaccines face the quartet challenge: Dengvaxia is approved only for those previously infected; TAK-003 is WHO-recommended for children 6–16 in high-transmission settings, regardless of prior infection, given in two doses; next-generation vaccines (including Brazilian efforts) are in development. Effective vaccines must elicit balanced neutralizing responses to all four serotypes and be part of tailored public health strategies.

The vectors are common in the Yangtze River basin and southern regions. Infection can occur after as little as 10 seconds of contact with contaminated water. The tail cercariae penetrate the skin, mature within snails, and are released into water, making affected waters high-risk. Incubation is about 40 days; early signs include skin rash, fever, and diarrhea. If untreated, schistosomiasis can progress to liver cirrhosis and ascites. Snails inhabit slow-moving, clear waters with vegetation along riverbanks, ditches, and reed beds. Prevention emphasizes avoiding suspected waters; workers should wear rubber boots and gloves, avoid handling snails with bare hands, and report sightings. Seek medical care promptly if symptoms develop after exposure and disclose exposure history.

articleSummary: TB detection in India is transitioning from smear microscopy to molecular tests, with GeneXpert (Cepheid) and Truenat (Molbio Diagnostics) delivering TB and rifampicin-resistance results in 1–2 hours and now approved as frontline tests under WHO and India’s National TB Elimination Programme. India’s 2025 TB elimination goal remains a work in progress, hinging on faster rollout.

International reports warn of potential reinfection, but there is not yet strong evidence of increased severity compared with Omicron subvariants. Indonesia’s Health Ministry reported no confirmed Cicada cases as of 8 April 2026, while mobility and surveillance dynamics demand vigilance.

articleSummary: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is highly contagious in Hue City, Vietnam, with 56 cases year-to-date reported by the Hue City CDC: 54 clinical, 2 laboratory-confirmed. Thuận Hóa and An Cựu wards each report 5 cases. The rise from 45 cases in the same period of 2025 represents a 24.4% increase. Transitional weather with variable temperature and humidity, plus crowding in preschools and playgrounds, facilitate spread. HFMD is caused by enteroviruses and transmits via saliva, nasal secretions, vesicle fluid, feces, and contaminated surfaces or toys. Coxsackievirus A16 was confirmed in one sample; Enterovirus 71 and other Coxsackie A6/A10 strains are also circulating and can cause severe CNS and cardiac complications if untreated. Samples were sent to Pasteur Institute Nha Trang for typing. Public health actions include proactive surveillance, 24–48 hour outbreak investigations, isolation, school measures, hygiene (3 clean practices: clean eating, clean living, clean hands), and possible temporary school closures to cut transmission.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Ticks enter their active season — what should you do after being bitten? What is "tick disease"? What are the symptoms? Be wary of the threat of acute infectious diseases.
articleHeadline: 蜱虫进入活跃期，被叮咬后怎么办？何为"蜱虫病"？有何症状？ 警惕急性传染病威胁
articleSummary: Tick-borne disease in China is caused by a novel bunyavirus and spread by tick bites. It presents with fever and thrombocytopenia, and may include nausea, vomiting, poor appetite, myalgia, fatigue, and headache; severe cases can include altered consciousness and multi-organ dysfunction, sometimes requiring ICU care. First reported in 2009, incidence is rising with wider geographic spread. The disease is classified as a Class B infectious disease to bolster surveillance and prevention. Ticks can carry multiple pathogens, causing Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, and tick-borne encephalitis. Ticks are most active in mountains and hills; peak season runs from 4 to 10 months. High-risk groups include outdoor workers, forest workers, and tea-pickers, especially with underlying conditions. After a bite, do not crush or twist; wipe the tick with alcohol, remove the mouthparts with tweezers, disinfect the wound, and observe for about a week; seek care if fever or redness develops.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Brazil becomes the first country in the world to make available an innovative malaria treatment for children - Jornal O Sul.
articleHeadline: Brasil se torna o 1º país no mundo a disponibilizar tratamento inovador contra a malária para crianças - Jornal O Sul
articleSummary: Brazil becomes the first country to offer tafenoquine in a pediatric formulation (50 mg) for malaria under the SUS, for children 10–35 kg. Delivery began March 2, 2026; 126,120 tablets were initially allocated with R$970,000 invested, and 64,800 tablets remain for distribution in high-incidence areas including Yanomami DSEI, Alto Rio Negro, Rio Tapajós, Manaus, Vale do Javari, and Médio Rio Solimões e Afluentes, with Yanomami DSEI receiving 14,550 tablets first. The single-dose regimen aims to improve adherence, reduce relapses, and curb transmission, in line with WHO recommendations. In 2024, tafenoquine 150 mg was introduced for patients >16 years in Yanomami. The program follows Brazil’s Amazon malaria control efforts, where 2025 data show the lowest case numbers since 1979 (15% national decline; 16% in Indigenous areas; 30% fewer Plasmodium falciparum cases), supported by increased diagnostics (Yanomami: tests +103.7%, diagnoses +116.6%) and a 70% reduction in malaria deaths in Yanomami. The initiative expands vector-control measures and public health reach in remote regions.
